title: Maximal Square
directAnswer: Let dp[i][j] be the side length of the largest all-1 square whose bottom-right corner is (i, j). If the cell is '1', dp[i][j] = min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) + 1; if it's '0', dp[i][j] = 0. Track the global max side and return side². Brute force is O((mn)²); the DP is O(mn) time, compressible to O(n) space with a single rolling row.

remember.pattern: 2D grid DP — square side from three neighbours
rules: dp[i][j] is the **side length of the largest square ending at (i, j) as its bottom-right corner** — not the area, not a boolean.
The recurrence is `min` of the three neighbours **plus one** — a square can only grow if top, left, AND diagonal all support the same smaller square.
Return the **area** (side × side), not the side itself — the prompt asks for the count of cells.
A `'0'` cell forces `dp = 0`: no square can end on an empty cell, which naturally resets the run.
The grid holds **characters** `'0'`/`'1'`, not ints — compare against `'1'`, not `1`.
whenToUse: Finding the largest axis-aligned square / region in a binary matrix
Each cell's answer depends on its up, left, and up-left neighbours
The shape you want is built incrementally from smaller versions of itself
You can define a state 'best thing ending exactly here' over a grid
antiSignals: You need the largest rectangle, not square → Maximal Rectangle via histogram stacks
Counting all squares of every size → still DP but sum the dp values instead of maxing
The region need not be contiguous / axis-aligned → connected components or geometry
Only the perimeter or a path matters → different DP or BFS
remember.takeaway: Maximal Square is the canonical 'min of three neighbours + 1' grid DP. The leap is defining dp as 'largest square ending HERE' so a 2D shape collapses into a 1-cell-at-a-time recurrence. The same `min(top, left, diag)+1` idea reappears in Count Square Submatrices and underlies the intuition for many matrix DPs.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can invent the right state definition — 'largest square ending at (i, j)' — and justify why the recurrence is the MIN of three neighbours, not the sum or the max.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to track squares by their top-left corner (which breaks the recurrence), using max instead of min over the neighbours, or returning the side length instead of the area.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain WHY min: a square of side k+1 ending here requires three overlapping squares of side k. Then compress to O(n) space by overwriting a single row and carefully saving the diagonal.

problemStatement:
Given an `m x n` binary `matrix` filled with `0`s and `1`s, find the largest **square** containing only `1`s and return ***its area***.

The matrix entries are given as the characters `'0'` and `'1'`.
understanding: Find the side of the biggest solid square of 1s anywhere in the grid, then report its area. The square must be axis-aligned and fully filled with 1s — a single 1 is a valid square of side 1 (area 1).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Square or rectangle?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Square — equal sides. If it were any rectangle, that's Maximal Rectangle (LC 85), solved with a histogram + monotonic stack.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want the area or the side length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The area. If the largest side is k, the answer is k². A common slip is returning k.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the cells integers or characters?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Characters '0' and '1'. Comparing against the int 1 silently fails — every cell looks like a 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the grid be all zeros?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Then no square exists and the answer is 0. The DP handles this because every dp cell stays 0.

examples.explanation: The largest all-1 square has side 2 (the block around rows 1-2, cols 2-3), so the area is 2² = 4.
No 2×2 square of 1s exists, but single 1s do, so the largest side is 1 and the area is 1.
A lone 0 — no square of 1s at all, so the area is 0.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Test Every Square
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to anchor the problem, then flag it as far too slow for a 300×300 grid before pivoting to DP.
hints: Forget cleverness first: how would you verify a square of a given size exists? Pick a top-left corner and a side length, then check every cell inside is a 1.
For each cell that is a '1', try to grow the largest square whose top-left corner sits there, expanding the side by one as long as the new row and column are all 1s.
Track the biggest valid side seen across all corners; the answer is that side squared.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are mn candidate corners; each may expand a square up to side min(m, n), and validating one expansion step scans O(side) new cells — overall roughly O(mn · min(m,n)²) in the worst case (an all-1s grid). No extra storage beyond a few counters.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal reading: a square of 1s is defined by a corner and a side, so enumerate corners and sides and check whether the cells inside are all 1. The cleanest version fixes each cell as the *top-left* corner and grows the square one ring at a time — to go from side `k` to side `k+1` you only need to confirm the new bottom row and right column of the larger square are all 1s.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** The problem literally asks for a square of 1s; brute force just makes 'a square of 1s' executable. No insight about subproblems is required — you mechanically try every possibility and keep the best. Stating it shows you understand the goal before optimizing.

**Why it collapses at scale.** The grid can be 300×300 = 90,000 cells, and an all-1s grid lets every corner expand a square up to side 300. The repeated re-scanning of overlapping regions is pure wasted work — the square you validate for one corner shares almost all its cells with the square for the corner next to it, yet brute force re-checks them from scratch. That redundancy is the tell that a DP is hiding here.

**The bridge to DP.** Notice that whether a big square *ends* at a cell is almost entirely determined by whether slightly smaller squares end at its neighbours. That overlap — answers that reuse answers one cell over — is exactly what dynamic programming exploits. State the brute force, name its redundancy, then define a per-cell state to remove it.
approaches.insight: Every brute-force validation re-examines cells its neighbour already examined. When the work for one position overlaps almost entirely with the position beside it, stop enumerating shapes and start defining a per-cell state — that reframe is the whole jump from brute force to grid DP.

approaches.name: 2D Bottom-Up DP — Min of Three Neighbours
approaches.whenToMention: The core insight they're testing. Lead with the state definition: 'dp[i][j] = side of the largest square whose bottom-right corner is (i, j)'.
hints: Define dp[i][j] as the side of the largest all-1 square whose BOTTOM-RIGHT corner sits at (i, j). What does it take for that square to have side k?
A square of side k+1 ending at (i, j) requires three squares of side k ending at the cell above, the cell to the left, and the cell diagonally up-left — all simultaneously.
So if grid[i][j]=='1', dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]); else 0. Track the global max side and return its square.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One O(1) recurrence evaluation per cell over an m×n grid = O(mn) time. The full dp table stores one int per cell = O(mn) space.
approaches.explanation:
The unlock is the **state definition**: let `dp[i][j]` be the side length of the largest all-1 square whose *bottom-right* corner is exactly `(i, j)`. Anchoring squares by their bottom-right corner (not top-left) is what makes the recurrence look only *backwards* — at up, left, and up-left — cells we've already computed when scanning top-to-bottom, left-to-right.

**Why the recurrence is `min` of three neighbours, plus one.** Suppose `(i, j)` is a 1 and we want the biggest square ending there. For a square of side `k+1` to fit, three smaller squares of side `k` must all exist: one ending directly above (covers the top of the new square), one ending to the left (covers its left side), and one ending diagonally up-left (covers its interior). The new square can only be as large as the *weakest* of those three supports allows — hence `min`, not `max` or sum. Add 1 for the current cell itself. If any neighbour can only support a side-`k` square, the diagonal corner of a side-`(k+1)` square would poke into a 0, so `min` correctly clamps it.

**The base case and the reset.** The first row and first column have no top/left/diagonal neighbour, so a 1 there can only ever be a square of side 1 — handled by treating out-of-bounds neighbours as 0. A `'0'` cell sets `dp[i][j] = 0`: no square can end on an empty cell, and this naturally resets any run, so we never need to clear state manually.

**Evaluation order and the final answer.** Because each cell depends only on cells above and to the left, a simple row-major double loop guarantees every dependency is ready before we read it. We don't return `dp[m-1][n-1]` — the biggest square can end anywhere — so we track a running `maxSide` across all cells and return `maxSide²` for the area.
approaches.insight: The entire problem hinges on choosing 'square ending at this cell as its bottom-right corner' as the state. That phrasing converts a global 2D search into a local recurrence reading three already-computed neighbours. Whenever a grid problem feels global, ask: 'what's the best thing ending exactly here?' — defining the answer per-cell is the heart of grid DP.

edgeCases.behavior: Every cell is '0', so dp stays all 0 and maxSide = 0 → area 0.
No cell has a top neighbour, so min is always 0 → every dp is 1, maxSide = 1, area = 1.

pitfalls: Using max instead of min over the three neighbours — overcounts squares that don't actually fit.
Anchoring the square at its top-left corner — forces forward dependencies and breaks the scan order.
Returning dp[m][n] instead of the tracked maxSide — the largest square rarely ends in the last cell.

approaches.name: Space-Optimized DP — One Rolling Row (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The polish that turns O(mn) space into O(n). Frame it as 'each cell only needs the row above and one diagonal value, so a single row plus a saved corner suffices'.
hints: Look at the recurrence: dp[i][j] only reads the row above (dp[i-1][*]) and the current row to the left. Do you really need all m rows in memory?
Keep just one 1D array of length n+1 and overwrite it row by row. The catch: dp[i-1][j-1] (the diagonal) gets clobbered the moment you compute dp[i][j-1].
Save the diagonal in a 'prev' variable before overwriting each cell: capture the old value, compute the new one, then carry the old value forward as the next diagonal.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Same O(mn) cell visits and O(1) work each. Storage is one array of n+1 ints plus a couple of scalars → O(n) space, independent of m.
approaches.explanation:
The 2D table never reads more than one row back, so we can collapse it to a **single rolling row** of length `n+1` that we overwrite in place as we move down the grid. Before processing row `i`, the array holds row `i-1`; after the inner loop, it holds row `i`.

**The one subtlety: the diagonal gets overwritten.** In the full table, `dp[i][j]` needs `dp[i-1][j-1]` — the up-left diagonal. But in a single array, by the time we reach column `j` we've already overwritten index `j-1` with the *current* row's value, destroying the diagonal we need. The fix is a single scalar, `prev`, that remembers the value at index `j-1` *from the previous row* just before we overwrite it. The dance per cell is: stash `temp = dp[j]` (the old top, which becomes the next iteration's diagonal), compute the new `dp[j]` using `prev` as the diagonal, then set `prev = temp`.

**Why this ordering is exact, not approximate.** `dp[j]` before assignment is `dp[i-1][j]` (top); `dp[j-1]` after the previous iteration is `dp[i][j-1]` (left); and `prev` holds `dp[i-1][j-1]` (diagonal). All three are precisely the values the 2D recurrence reads — we've just stored them in three live slots instead of an entire matrix. Reset `prev = 0` at the start of each row so the leftmost column correctly sees a zero diagonal.

**Why it matters.** For a 300×300 grid the table is trivial, but the rolling-row pattern is a transferable skill: whenever a 2D DP's recurrence reaches back only one row, it compresses to O(n) space with a saved-diagonal trick. This same compression turns Unique Paths, Minimum Path Sum, and Edit Distance into single-row solutions.
approaches.insight: When a 2D recurrence only looks one row up, you don't need the whole grid — one row plus a saved diagonal scalar is enough. The trick is recognizing that overwriting in place destroys exactly one needed value (the diagonal), so you preserve it in a single temp before each write. That 'stash-then-overwrite' move is the constant-space signature of one-row-back grid DPs.

pitfalls: Forgetting prev = 0 at the start of each row — the leftmost cell inherits a stale diagonal and overcounts.
Reading dp[j] as the diagonal instead of the top — dp[j] before assignment is the top (row above), not the diagonal.
Not resetting dp[j] to 0 on a '0' cell — a stale value from the row above leaks through and corrupts later cells.

commonMistakes: Using max instead of min over the three neighbours — the recurrence requires ALL three supports, so the smallest caps the new side.
Returning the side length instead of side² — the prompt asks for area.
Comparing cells to the int 1 instead of the char '1' — every cell reads as 0 and the answer is always 0.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Max instead of min over neighbours
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A square of side k+1 needs the top, left, AND diagonal squares to all be at least side k. Taking the max assumes one strong neighbour is enough and reports squares that don't actually fit.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning side instead of area
commonMistakesDetailed.why: dp tracks side lengths; the problem wants the number of cells, which is side². Returning maxSide passes tiny cases by luck and fails the moment the largest side exceeds 1.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing to int 1 instead of char '1'
commonMistakesDetailed.why: LeetCode passes the grid as characters. matrix[i][j] == 1 compares a char to an int and is always false, so dp stays all zeros.

followupVariations.hint: Same min-of-three recurrence, but SUM all dp values instead of maxing — each dp[i][j] also counts how many squares end there.

patternNote: Canonical 2D grid DP with a 'best shape ending at this cell' state. Recognize it when each cell's answer is built from its up/left/diagonal neighbours. Same min(top, left, diag)+1 shape powers Count Square Submatrices; the broader 'state ending here over a grid' idea drives Minimum Path Sum, Unique Paths, and Edit Distance.
